gen.title: New key pair
gen.body: An SSH key is a pair of files: the private one stays on this PC, the public one is added to the server. Key login is safer than a password, and you won't have to type the password on every connection.
gen.location: An Ed25519 key will be created by the system ssh-keygen in the ~/.ssh folder on this PC.

missing.title: ssh-keygen was not found on this PC
missing.body: Creating a key requires the Windows "OpenSSH Client" component. It is usually preinstalled, but it could not be found here.
missing.how: To enable it: Settings → System → Optional features → "Add a feature" → "OpenSSH Client" → Install. Then reopen this wizard.

pass.title: Passphrase — a password for the key file itself
pass.body: If the key file is stolen, it cannot be used without the passphrase. You will need to enter it when connecting. You can leave it empty — then login will require no typing at all.
pass.helper: Stored in Windows Credential Manager after saving the host — like passwords
pass.error: Could not set the passphrase — the key remains without one. You can continue and set it later with ssh-keygen -p.

pub.title: Public key
pub.body: This line is safe to show and share — it is what gets added to the server. Never send the private key file to anyone.

install.title: Adding the key to the server
install.body: On the first connection to this host, enter the server password — LucidSSH will add the public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server automatically. After that, login will use the key, no password needed.
install.note: The form has already been switched to the new key — just save the host and connect.

welcome.title: Welcome to LucidSSH

fp.bodyFirst: Make sure the fingerprint matches what your hosting provider shows.
fp.explain: A fingerprint is the server's digital thumbprint. It confirms you are connecting to your own server.
fp.bodyChanged: The saved fingerprint of “{{host}}” does not match the new one. This happens after a server reinstall or update, but may also mean a man-in-the-middle attack. Verify the new fingerprint via an independent source: hosting panel or server console.

fp.whereToFindText: If your hosting provider shows the fingerprint (e.g. in the server console) — compare it against this one. If it doesn't — that's normal for many hosting providers, and you can trust this connection. If the fingerprint changes later, LucidSSH will block the connection and warn you.

explain.rm-recursive: This command deletes “{{target}}” with all its contents. This action is irreversible.
explain.dd-write: dd will overwrite “{{target}}” — all data on it will be lost beyond recovery.
explain.mkfs: mkfs will create a new filesystem on “{{target}}”, erasing all data on the device.
explain.chmod-777: chmod -R 777 makes “{{target}}” and everything inside readable and writable by everyone — a serious security hole.
explain.truncate: truncate will empty the file “{{target}}”, erasing its contents.
explain.redirect-device: Writing directly to device “{{target}}” will corrupt its filesystem.
explain.shred: shred overwrites “{{target}}” repeatedly, making the data unrecoverable.
explain.wipefs: wipefs erases the filesystem signatures on “{{target}}” — the device becomes unreadable.
explain.fork-bomb: This is a fork bomb: it spawns processes exponentially and freezes the server.
explain.drop-database: This command irreversibly drops the database or table “{{target}}”.
explain.kill-init: Signaling process 1 (init/systemd) will crash the whole system.
explain.generic: This command is recognized as potentially destructive. Review it before running.

accessRisk.title: Risk of losing SSH access

explain.sshd-config: This command modifies the SSH server configuration. A mistake in the config may make the server unreachable over SSH after the service restarts.
explain.firewall: This command changes firewall rules. A bad rule may block the SSH port and drop the connection to the server.
explain.passwd: This command changes a user's password. If the new password is lost or mistyped, password login may become impossible.
explain.sshd-service: This command stops or restarts the SSH service. If the service fails to come back up, you won't be able to reconnect over SSH.

accessRisk.recommendation: Recommendation: before running this, open a second tab with a new connection to this server and make sure it works before closing the current session.
accessRisk.sshdTest: After editing the config, validate it with sshd -t before restarting the service.

start.title: Welcome to LucidSSH
start.body: LucidSSH is a safe SSH client for everyday server work. Manage connections, keep commands at hand, and don't fear dangerous operations — the Guard warns in advance and the error detector tells you what to check.
start.item1: Add a server: click + in the Servers panel and enter address, port and credentials.
start.item2: Connect: double-click a server or drag it onto the tabs.
start.item3: Work: type commands right in the terminal; the path above is clickable.
start.fingerprintTitle: How to verify a server's fingerprint
start.fingerprintIntro: A fingerprint is a short digest of the server's key that confirms you're connecting to your own server, not an impostor.
start.fingerprintWhereVps: VPS hosting (DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Vultr, Timeweb and similar) — open the server's web console ("Console" / "VNC") in the control panel and reboot the server: the fingerprint appears in the boot log.
start.fingerprintWhereAws: AWS EC2 — "Get system log" in the instance monitoring section.
start.fingerprintWhereSelf: Your own server, home NAS, Raspberry Pi — run this on the server itself:
start.fingerprintFallback: If you couldn't find it anywhere — that's normal, many budget hosting providers don't publish the fingerprint. In that case you can trust the first connection. LucidSSH will remember this fingerprint and warn you if it changes on future connections — protecting you from server impersonation later, even if you can't verify it now.
start.quickConnectTitle: Quick Connect without saving a host
start.quickConnectIntro: For a one-off connection — say, to check out a new server — you don't need to add it to the list. Enter the address as user@host or user@host:port (e.g. root@192.0.2.10:2222), and LucidSSH connects right away.
start.quickConnectWaysLabel: You can open Quick Connect four ways:
start.quickConnectWay1: the ⚡ button in the servers panel header
start.quickConnectWay3: the "connect directly" link on the no-active-session screen
start.quickConnectWay4: just start typing user@host in the server search box — a "Connect" item appears as the first result
start.quickConnectSaveNote: This kind of connection isn't saved to the server list. After the session, LucidSSH offers to save the server as a host — accept if you plan to connect again: the password goes into Windows' protected credential store, and the server appears in the list on the left.
start.quickConnectFingerprintNote: Fingerprint verification works here too: on first connect you'll see the same confirmation prompt as for saved hosts.

saved.title: Saved commands
saved.body: Frequently used commands can be saved as snippets and run in one click.
saved.item1: Save: 🔖 in history or right-click in the terminal → Save as snippet.
saved.item1PasteMode: Save: 🔖 in history. Right-click in the terminal is set to paste from the clipboard (Settings → Terminal).
saved.item2: Scope: server snippets show only on that connection, global ones everywhere.
saved.item3: Run: from the catalog [host]/Global tabs (Ctrl+L) — drag to reorder there too.
saved.item4: Quick-insert: Ctrl+Space next to the cursor opens a floating snippet search right in the terminal.

guard.title: Dangerous command guard
guard.body: Before destructive commands (rm -rf, kill -9, mkfs and similar) the Guard shows a confirmation requiring the object name — accidental deletion is prevented.
guard.item1: Interception happens before the command is sent to the server.
guard.item2: You must type the exact object name or a confirmation word — not just OK.
guard.item3: Can be disabled globally in Settings → Security.
guard.item4: For risky but non-destructive commands (editing sshd_config, firewall rules and similar) — a softer Continue/Cancel warning, no name required.

error.title: Error detector
error.body: When a command fails, a panel slides up with a plain explanation and what-to-check steps — offline, no cloud.
error.item1: Triggers on a non-zero exit code or an error message.
error.item2: Steps can be inserted into the input or copied in one click.
error.item3: The panel doesn't cover the input; close with Esc or ×.
